input:
It is worth noting that heat exchanger calculations often require a representative temperature driving force, and in this example we will explore how the log-mean temperature difference can be determined for a countercurrent exchanger. The process stream is cooled from 200 °C to 150 °C, while the cooling water enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. It should be emphasised that the temperature difference between the two streams is not constant throughout the exchanger, which is precisely why a logarithmic mean is utilised instead of a simple average. The log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, is related to the terminal differences $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ through the following well-known expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

By substituting the terminal differences of 125 K and 110 K into this expression, the log-mean temperature difference is found to be 117.3 K. Interestingly, this value lies between the two terminal differences and, notably, closer to the smaller of the two, highlighting the characteristic behaviour of the logarithmic mean. Furthermore, it is important to remember that this result is based on certain key assumptions, namely that the overall coefficient remains constant along the exchanger and that neither stream undergoes a phase change during the process. If a stream were to condense or boil, the temperature profile would change significantly, and the calculated value would no longer provide an accurate representation of the behaviour of the exchanger, underscoring the importance of checking the assumptions carefully in practice.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C. Cooling water enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C, flowing against the process stream. The hot stream gives up heat along the full length of the surface, and its temperature falls steadily from inlet to outlet. Because the temperature difference between the streams varies along the exchanger, one mean difference must stand for the whole surface in a duty calculation. For the hot-end difference $\Delta T_1$, the cold-end difference $\Delta T_2$ and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$, each in K, under a constant overall coefficient and with no phase change in either stream, the defining relation is

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

Substitution of the terminal differences, 125 K and 110 K, gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 117.3 K. The result sits between the two terminal differences and closer to the smaller one. That position is the check on the calculation: the logarithmic mean of two unequal differences always falls below their arithmetic mean, because the temperature gap narrows along the path the hot stream takes and the narrower stretches contribute less driving force per unit of surface. An arithmetic mean of the same two differences would overstate the driving force and undersize the exchanger. The duty calculation that follows from the value inherits both assumptions, and a design that relaxes either one must return to the temperature profile rather than to the mean difference alone. Where a stream condenses or boils, the temperature of that stream holds while its partner stream changes, the profile departs from the form the relation assumes, and the log-mean temperature difference is no longer the mean the duty calculation needs.
